canonical_statement: The study tests whether outcome-only reinforcement learning fails to train mid-episode skill selection because selection tokens receive too little and often wrong-signed credit, and evaluates a token-local alternative called SkillGate.

Evaluation uses five agentic benchmarks with a 16-candidate mixed skill slate containing one verified oracle skill, five misleading hard negatives, five relevant bystanders, and five irrelevant bystanders.
Training uses 491 tasks with no Claw-Eval task; training and evaluation oracle skills are disjoint as skill identities.

Task outcome is evaluated on 385 trials: four repeats for each of 56 non-Claw tasks and one trial for each of 161 Claw-Eval tasks; detailed read behavior uses a 280-trial subset of 70 tasks with four repeats each.

All trained rows start from the same Qwen3.5-9B supervised-fine-tuned initialization; RL configurations run 100 on-policy GRPO steps with 8 rollouts per prompt, global batch 128, learning rate 1e-6, KL coefficient 3e-5, and SkillGate selector coefficient lambda 0.20.
SkillGate partitions credit into disjoint channels: task-outcome advantage applies only to execution tokens with the read call removed, while selector advantage applies only to skill-identity tokens.
The selector utility is positive only when a trajectory has exactly one attributed skill read and that read is the oracle; the utility is centered across read actions within the same prompt group.
Token weights are normalized so the task and selector channels each have total mass N when selector tokens are present, making selector weight independent of trajectory length.
On the 385-trial protocol, SkillGate achieved 53.2% overall trial success versus 47.0% for SkillRL outcome-only and 40.8% for the SFT RL initialization.

population.label: 385-trial protocol across Claw-Eval, SkillsBench, SETA, SWE, and Terminal-Bench 2.0

canonical_statement: On the same 385 trials, SkillGate read an oracle skill on 83.9% of trials versus 54.3% for SkillRL outcome-only.

canonical_statement: On the same 385 trials, SkillGate read a misleading skill on 21.8% of trials versus 69.6% for SkillRL outcome-only.

canonical_statement: In the 280-trial credit-design ablation, SkillGate achieved 50.0% trial success versus 42.1% for outcome-only SkillRL.
In the 280-trial ablation, clean single-oracle behavior occurred on 75.4% of SkillGate trials versus 21.4% with outcome-only SkillRL.
Action-local credit without the single-read constraint reached 45.0% trial success and 64.6% clean single-oracle behavior, while SkillGate reached 50.0% and 75.4%, respectively.

On the 280-trial external-selection comparison, SkillGate reached 50.0% trial success, compared with 36.8% for a Qwen3.5-27B external router feeding the frozen SFT executor and 48.2% for oracle-only injection into that executor.

canonical_statement: In task-clustered bootstrap analysis of the repeated-trial protocol, SkillGate improved pooled trial success over outcome-only SkillRL by 7.9 percentage points, with a 95% interval of +2.1 to +14.3 points.
For pooled task pass@4, the SkillGate minus outcome-only difference was 7.1 percentage points with a 95% interval of -1.4 to +15.7 points; the authors did not claim significance for pass@4.
Each training configuration is represented by a single run.
SkillGate requires training tasks for which the correct skill is known.
The action-local selector scheme cannot directly credit abstention.
The paper reports public code at github.com/DeepExperience/SkillGate and a SkillGate-9B model at huggingface.co/simonlqy/SkillGate-9B.

The authors conclude that selector learning and execution learning should be trained separately at the token-credit level when consequential mid-trajectory choices occupy only a small span of a long rollout.
